title: We Are the Marauders
author: John Feffer
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/sRRw6DoheMWkFgeTcVZTRX-680x383.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/04/we-
are-the-marauders/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/sRRw6DoheMWkFgeTcVZTRX-680x383.jpg)

Still from Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey.

About 3,300 years ago, in the region around the Mediterranean, civilization
collapsed. That’s what the archaeological record shows: the spectacular
disappearance of a number of thriving cultures in Greece, Anatolia, and the
Middle East. The Minoan palaces, with their astonishing frescoes of acrobats
jumping over bulls, fell into ruins. Cyprus, at the crossroads of late Bronze
Age culture, suffered a series of devastating attacks. Powerful Egypt was
hobbled.

Perhaps the most famous destruction, however, took place at the city of Troy,
which was part of the Hittite empire that stretched across modern-day Turkey.
The fall of Troy is, of course, the subject of the two great works of ancient
Greek poetry: the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_. Composed sometime between 725 and
675 BC, or nearly half a millennium after the events they describe, the works
attributed to the blind poet Homer recount the decade-long Greek siege of
Troy, the clever ploy developed by Odysseus to smuggle soldiers into the city
by way of a “gift” of a massive wooden horse, and then the 10-year journey of
Odysseus back to his wife and child in Ithaca.

What the books do not detail is what ultimately happened to the conquerors
after the sack of Troy. The Mycenaean civilization—the disparate Greek city-
states that united at the end of the Bronze Age to sail against Troy in the
_Iliad_ —suffered the same fate as the great city of Priam and Hector. Athens,
Thebes, Pylos: they all became rubble. It was only in Homer’s time that Greece
was able to make a comeback.

The culprits responsible for the collapse of Troy are well-known. But what
about the other civilizations? Inscriptions from late Bronze Age Egypt mention
a mysterious “sea people” marauding through the region and destroying the
great cities of Hatti, Ugarit, and Ascalon. The people of the sea very nearly
bring down the Egyptians as well but are defeated in two epic battles.
Weakened by war and other factors, Egypt goes into decline.

These “sea people” figure prominently in Christopher Nolan’s latest film, _The
Odyssey_. As Odysseus makes his way back to Ithaca, he encounters rumors that
these mysterious marauders have put everyone up and down the coast on alert.
At a key moment in the film, Odysseus comes to a startling realization.
Reflecting on the pillage of Troy and his voyage of slaughter back home to
Ithaca, Odysseus understands that he and his fellow Greeks are, in fact, the
notorious sea people.

It is a supremely ahistorical gloss on the source text. The Mycenean Greeks,
after all, were also victims of the “sea people.” The _Iliad,_ rather than
mourn the bloodshed, celebrates the Greek victory over Troy. In the _Odyssey_
, the eponymous character seems to show little if any regret about his role in
the city’s destruction. Indeed, he seems to have little regard for the
consequences of any of his actions, an obtuseness parodied to great effect by
a tart-tongued Penelope in the Natalie Haynes novel [_A Thousand
Ships_](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/a-thousand-ships-natalie-haynes
"A Thousand Ships").

But Nolan was not aiming for historical or literary accuracy. It would have
been a fool’s errand, in any case. He was making a film about a poetic
retelling of a legend whose details had been tumbled and polished by
innumerable bards over the centuries. Much of the controversy around the film,
fueled by the “anti-woke” polemics of the far right, have focused on the
casting. Should Nolan have found a Greek actor instead of Matt Damon to play
Odysseus? How to cast the goddess Athena or even the famed beauty Helen who
was the offspring of a god and a mortal? Are there really any actors out there
with a single eye in the middle of their forehead who could have pulled off
the role of Cyclops?

Modern historians no longer think that the “sea people” were solely
responsible for the decline of so many powerful entities. Probably climate
change [played a role](https://www.gu.se/en/research/the-collapse-of-bronze-
age-societies-in-the-eastern-mediterranean-sea-peoples-in-cyprus "played a
role"), with drought pushing regions to their ecological limits and prompting
people to take to the sea in search of fertile land. But Nolan was not
interested in making a documentary about the late Bronze Age collapse of Troy
and other cities. Rather, he was inspired by the gaps in the historical
record. “The people from the sea are essentially these marauders who some
believe brought about the collapse of civilization, but nobody knows their
lost history,” Nolan [told](https://www.vulture.com/article/christopher-nolan-
explains-the-key-to-the-odysseys-ending.html "told") _Vulture_. “Nobody knows
who they were, and there’s not a lot of information about it. There’s a lot of
speculation.”

Like any good filmmaker, Nolan had an axe to grind. In designing an epic anti-
war film, he turned Odysseus from a trickster into a brooder. The man behind
the Trojan Horse, like the subject of Nolan’s _Oppenheimer_ , has developed
second thoughts about his great technological breakthrough. Odysseus looks
upon the rape and pillage of Troy, brought about by the trick of the Trojan
Horse, much as Oppenheimer considered the consequences of the atomic bomb he
helped develop. Both technologies were used to end long conflicts; both
technologies stir regret on the part of their creators. After the atomic bombs
were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Oppenheimer confessed to President
Harry Truman that he, like the other scientists involved in the Manhattan
Project, [had blood on his
hands](https://contingentmagazine.org/2023/12/07/blood-on-our-hands/ "had
blood on his hands").

Nolan’s Odysseus goes one step further. During the 10-year voyage home
portrayed in the film, he mourns not only the men under his command who have
died but also the victims of the assault on Troy. In the film, even his
dispatch of the suitors who have been trying to win his wife Penelope’s hand
is bound up with his contrition for previous lives lost. In a substantial
departure from the text, Nolan sends his protagonist at the end of the film
into exile with his wife to atone for the deaths of his fighting companions.

Much is made in the film about the violation of _xenia_ , or the hospitality
that one must show to foreigners. This divine law is upheld by Penelope back
in Ithaca when she hosts all the scheming suitors, though several years of
eating and drinking at their host’s expense must surely violate the statute of
limitations on hospitality. Odysseus, meanwhile, flouts the law with his
Trojan Horse, though surely a war requires the suspension of any rule
requiring that hospitality be accorded to men with weapons.

For Nolan’s purposes, however, _xenia_ is a necessary counterpoint to
xenophobia, the hatred of strangers that pervades contemporary culture. A
little more xenia and a lot less xenophobia, the filmmaker suggests with his
script and his multicultural casting, would perhaps forestall the collapse of
civilization toward which the world is spinning. War, the ultimate violation
of hospitality shown to foreigners, is not an opportunity in the film to gain
glory but just the accumulation of dead bodies and blood-stained treasure.

Nolan is nodding at the headline news. In today’s environment, America,
Russia, and Israel have all used epic rationales for their murderous misdeeds.
Russia is defending its civilization, Israel is seeking revenge for a surprise
attack, and America is in search of lost greatness. They have identified the
dangerous marauders as terrorists of one stripe or another: Hamas, Hezbollah,
Venezuelans on boats, Iranian mullahs, Ukrainian Nazis.

These “heroic” nations have produced Iliads and Iliads of press releases,
tweets, and self-serving propaganda. But a self-aware Odysseus, like the one
portrayed by Nolan, is much harder to find. Dissenting Russians have gone into
exile. A handful of politicians have stood up to the U.S. war machine. It’s
the rare Israeli who challenges the colonial mindset of Zionism. Such a world
could certainly use more leaders who step down in order to go on a global
apology tour.

Nolan ends on a hopeful note about the fall and rise of civilizations. Yes,
the Bronze Age will come to an end, but then there will be Homer and the
glories of Athens just a few hundred years later. It’s reassuring to be
reminded that although civilizations come and go, history and humanity soldier
on.

But here’s the thing: the Greeks didn’t have nukes. Today, civilizations can
disappear just like Troy. But, after Oppenheimer, there’s a chance that they
might not come back.
